problem: Prior EQA datasets use rule-based or template queries that directly name target objects and properties (e.g. 'What color is the sofa?'). They cannot pose situational queries such as 'Is the house ready for sleeptime?', which need consensus over multiple object states.
motivation: A household robot will meet situational queries whose answers depend on generally accepted object states (lights off, doors closed). Collecting such queries in the real world is intrusive and cognitively heavy, so the authors use an LLM as a prior to generate them and ask whether LLMs can also answer them.
key_idea: A Prompt-Generate-Evaluate (PGE) loop makes GPT-4 generate unique situational queries with consensus object states and relationships, using clustering-based prompt feedback and similarity-triggered regeneration; the data is then validated by MTurk humans.
insight: GPT-4 generates authentic situational data (97.26% answerable on MTurk) but answers it poorly (46.2% correlation with humans, with reasoning that goes against commonsense). Object-level VQA on consensus queries beats room-level VQA on situational queries (about +15.31% accuracy on average), and 74.3% of MTurk users found consensus queries easier, so decomposing into consensus object states helps. In the real world, without a grounded scene graph, GPT-4V hallucinates ghost object states.
method: Situational query definition: queries must be abstract (no object words), contextual (need multiple object states) and binary Yes/No; these rules are given to the LLM in-context.
Datapoint generation: GPT-4 outputs [Query, Object-States, Object-Relationships]; the system prompt holds the VirtualHome scene graph (object states/relations) and 'do not conjure new objects'.

Generated Query Update: embed queries with RoBERTa, cluster them agglomeratively into k groups, put the query nearest each centroid into the system prompt as 'Generated Queries' to steer away from them.
Continued Conversation: compute cosine similarity of each new batch to the query database; if above a threshold, send a re-generation prompt stating the similarity percentage.

MTurk validation: 5 annotators per datapoint (Yes/No/Cannot Answer, majority vote; any Cannot Answer marks the datapoint unanswerable). A comparison study contrasts situational room queries with consensus object queries.

Evaluation: Room VQA (top-view images, situational query) and Object VQA (consensus query 'Is the OBJ STATE?') with BLIP-2/BLIP/ViLT, plus Joint scores; GPT-4 answers from the full scene graph, with reasoning prompts.
Real-world transfer: 10 lab images fed to GPT-4V within PGE to generate 100 datapoints, manually annotated.

setting.backbone: GPT-4 (frozen) for generation and answering; GPT-4V/4o for real-world; BLIP-2, BLIP, ViLT for VQA evaluation
setting.training_data: none (training-free prompting; the VQA models are used off-the-shelf)
setting.observation: VirtualHome scene graph (text), top-view room images and first-person object images; real-world RGB images
setting.action_space: none (question answering, no navigation actions evaluated)
setting.privileged: Fully observable VirtualHome scene graph given to the LLM for generation and answering

numbers_note: Not a navigation benchmark paper. Other reported figures: 97.26% answerable on MTurk, 46.2% GPT-4 correlation with humans (46.8% mismatch in Fig. 5 caption), 57.8% mismatch in the real world.
results: PGE generated 2K situational datapoints, 97.26% of which were answerable by MTurk annotators. GPT-4 correlates with human answers at only 46.2% (57.8% mismatch on real-world data). Object VQA (BLIP-2 58.26% acc) beats Room VQA (42.31%).
limitations: Saturation: the LLM starts generating near-duplicate queries, so generation was capped at 2K.
Real-world generation hallucinates ghost object states without a grounded scene graph.
VirtualHome's limited object set and synthetic images hurt VQA; the queries are mostly single-room and spatial, and no embodied agent navigates or explores.
